---
title: "Light Reflections"
author: "DK"
date: "2026-07-09"
categories: [independence]
---

These days, visiting a certain place has a way of conjuring up songs from the past.

At these locations, I realize that those who walked these same paths before me, created their own stories and soundtracks.

They have moved on, and eventually, so will I.

Places, time, events, and people—these are the classic triggers of nostalgia.

But when the moment passes, what actually remains?

The land and its designations will be owned, remembered, or renamed by the next generation.

Ultimately, the most lasting element isn't the geography or the event itself; it is the people.

If we make the conscious effort to remember them, their stories remain with us, providing a shortcut to wisdom.

Without those shared memories, we are forced to relearn hard lesson ourselves.

Thinking of those lessons and recent visits to the northern part of Western United States brought to mind a song written by an Irish rock band back in 1987, capturing their impressions of the United States.

Specifically, a song about life in "God’s Country" seemed to fit my mood well. But as the initial impact of the music faded, another thought took hold:

> Why do I rely on anthems written for the masses to define my most personal moments?

I have access to the same creative tools they had. I even have a set of tools they didn't have—access to LLM-based assistance.

Instead of searching for an existing track that merely suits the moment, I could create something that truly fits me: the exact mood, the specific place, and the unique feeling.

While choosing to create rather than consume is undoubtedly the more difficult route, it feels like the right path forward.

![](images/20260702_205858 (1)-01.jpg)

---

This thought stayed with me as I walked around the grounds of the state capital, passing an equestrian statue featuring one of its prominent historic citizens.

A few blocks away stood the cathedral named after the very person who started the war between the Greeks and the Trojans.

Across the way sat Temple Emanu-El, as well as the First Presbyterian Church.

On the west side of the church was a beautiful stained-glass window.

Because the building was closed, the motif and the story told by the glass were initially unattainable.

However, as I approached the building, a figure emerged as a portion of the window was illuminated.

The image was that of the young Jesus Christ, conversing with the wise men of his day at the temple while his parents were traveling home.

At first, I assumed the setting sun had hit the stained glass at just the right angle.

But it was sunset, and since the building faced west, the sun could not be the source of illumination that created the image. There had to be another source.

I realized then the light was internal and an active source.

It was not a passive light relying on the time of day, but an active light from within, permanently fixated on the figure of Christ.

![](images/20260702_210323 (1).jpg)

---

Many have lived a life worthy of remembrance, and both physical monuments and apocryphal stories attest to their greatness.

The memories and associated soundtrack they created for the historical narrative is entirely worthy of our study and emulation.

However, at some point in our progression, rather than merely adhering to a certain branch of learning or becoming a disciple of someone else's study, it is far more worthwhile to compose our own soundtrack—one based on our unique background, upbringing, and what we personally stand for.

In the end, it is not what we leave behind hoping others might remember us, but what we create and take with us. That final act of individual creation might seem like a deeply solitary thing, but it is also the most rewarding.
